basis: trunk, excluding frontal appendages and tail fan
source: Daley & Edgecombe 2014, J. Paleontol. 88:68-91; maximum 38.7 cm in Lerosey-Aubril & Pates 2018
note: The largest known Cambrian animal in Whittington & Briggs 1985's title, and still the biggest thing on this roster. 0.5 m is the whole animal with appendages and tail fan; the trunk figure is the one that scales.

source: Lerosey-Aubril & Pates 2018, Nat. Commun. 9:3774 (22.8-33.6 cm); appendages described by Daley & Peel 2010, feeding by Vinther et al. 2014, Nature 507:496
note: Known from frontal appendages and a head shield, so the body length is reconstructed from relatives. Popular accounts of a 2 m filter feeder come from the 2014 press cycle, not from a measurement; the 2018 estimate is the one to use.

source: Moysiuk & Caron 2019, Proc. R. Soc. B 286:20191079
note: Hundreds of specimens; the carapace alone is the size of a hand. Second only to Anomalocaris here.

source: Moon, Caron & Moysiuk 2023, Proc. R. Soc. B 290:20222490 (182 specimens)
note: The oldest unequivocal swimming medusa. Bell width is about 40% of height and the ~90 tentacles add another 15%, so the swimming silhouette is taller than it is wide.

source: Briggs 1981, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 291:541; Izquierdo-Lopez & Caron 2024, Proc. R. Soc. B 291:20240622
note: One of the largest Cambrian bivalved arthropods. The 2024 redescription works from specimens near 20 cm.

source: Bruton 1981, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 295:619; Zacai et al. 2016 on the gut contents
note: One of the largest arthropods in the Walcott Quarry. Typical specimens 5-13 cm.

source: Caron, Scheltema, Schander & Rudkin 2006, Nature 442:159 (189 specimens)
note: A flat grazing oval with one muscular foot. The same radula-like apparatus as Wiwaxia, at more than twice the length.

source: Conway Morris 1977, Spec. Pap. Palaeontol. 20; Smith, Harvey & Butterfield 2015, Palaeontology 58:705
note: Specimens average about 8 cm; the largest reach 15. An extended proboscis adds to that without adding to the body.

source: Whittington 1975/1980 on the appendages; Losso, Hughes et al. 2025 on leg mobility
note: Adults commonly 5-7 cm, up to 9-10. A mid-sized animal here, which is roughly where a Burgess trilobite belongs.

source: Vannier, Aria, Taylor & Caron 2018, R. Soc. Open Sci. 5:172206
note: Shrimp-shaped under a folded carapace, and the earliest animal known to brood eggs.

source: Hou 1987; Shu et al. 2001, Nature 414:419 (Chengjiang)
note: Not a Burgess animal: Chengjiang, and about 8 million years older than the rest of the roster.

source: Conway Morris & Caron 2012, Biol. Rev. 87:480 (114 specimens); range 1.5-6 cm
note: Averages about 5 cm. Reoriented the other way up by Mussini et al. 2024, which does not change the length.

basis: body, excluding the trailing whips of the great appendages
source: Bruton & Whittington 1983, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 300:553; Haug, Briggs & Haug 2012, BMC Evol. Biol. 12:162
note: The great appendages carry long flagella that roughly double the animal's reach without adding body.

source: Whittington 1975, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 271:1 (range 4-7 cm)
note: The proboscis adds about a third again to the reach and nothing to the body.

source: Smith & Caron 2010, Nature 465:469; Smith 2013, Paleobiology 39:297
note: Two size morphs, anatomically identical: a small one around 2.5 cm and a large one near four times that. The mid figure covers both.

basis: body height, comb rows along it
source: Conway Morris & Collins 1996, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 351:279
note: 24 comb rows, three times a modern ctenophore's eight. Specimen figures cluster near 3.4 cm.

basis: whole animal, sclerites included, spines excluded
source: Conway Morris 1985, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 307:507; Smith 2014, Palaeontology 57:215
note: Most specimens are 1-3 cm; the dorsal spines stand well clear of that and are not counted in the length.

source: Conway Morris 1979, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 285:227; Parry & Caron 2019, Proc. R. Soc. B 286:20191247
note: The iridescent bristles are longer than the body is wide, and are not part of the length.

source: Vannier, Garcia-Bellido, Hu & Chen 2009, Proc. R. Soc. B 276:2567; Legg & Vannier 2013, Acta Palaeontol. Pol. 54:699 on the Burgess species
note: The spines at each end add roughly half again to the outline and nothing to the animal.

source: Smith & Caron 2015, Nature 523:75; Conway Morris 1977 (range 0.5-5.5 cm)
note: The seven pairs of dorsal spines stand about as tall as the body is long, so the drawn silhouette is far bigger than the length.

source: Garcia-Bellido & Collins 2006, Can. J. Earth Sci. 43:721 (range 2.4-24.5 mm, >25000 specimens)
note: The commonest animal in the Burgess Shale and the smallest on this roster. The four swept spines make it look larger than it measures.
